findings.title: Global rate limiter caps production traffic at 100 req/min per IP while one page view costs 4-16 requests; 429s are never retried, so throttled writes are dropped
findings.evidence: Measured: autocannon 8.0.0, 30s at concurrency 10 against GET /api/documents?type=wiki returned 511,872 responses of which 511,872 were HTTP 429 and 0 were 2xx (statusCodeStats {"429":{"count":511872}}) — the limiter, not the application, is the binding throughput constraint, and the entire benchmark had to be re-architected into rate-limit-window-synchronised bursts to obtain any valid latency data. Browser trace of the config userFlows (headless Chromium, logged in as dev@ship.local) recorded 63 /api requests across 8 flows (49 unique): login 16, dashboard 12, document view 10, sprint board 10. Production limit is max: 100 per 60s window per IP (api/src/app.ts:83 evaluates isTestEnv=false, isDevEnv=false in production). Client side, `grep -rn "429" web/src` returns zero matches, and both retry predicates return false for every status in [400,500).
findings.hypothesis: The 100 req/min ceiling was sized as if one page view were one request, but this SPA issues 4-16 XHRs per navigation, so a single user exhausts the window after roughly 6-10 navigations per minute. In the deployed topology (CloudFront -> Elastic Beanstalk, app.ts:93 sets trust proxy 1) every user behind one agency NAT egress collapses to a single rate-limit key, so a team shares one 100 req/min budget collectively. Because react-query treats 429 as a non-retryable 4xx for mutations as well as queries, a throttled PATCH of document metadata (title, state, priority, assignee) fails permanently and surfaces only as a toast; Yjs editor body text survives because /collaboration WebSocket traffic is not behind the /api/ limiter, but metadata writes are.
findings.estimatedImpact: Raising the limit to a per-page-view-realistic value (or keying it per session rather than per IP) removes an artificial ~1.7 req/s prod ceiling and stops silent write loss. Until it is fixed no latency optimisation is observable in production, because the limiter bounds throughput far below anything measured here (299-900 req/s). Cross-reference: the dropped-write path should be reproduced end-to-end by error-handling-audit (ERR).

findings.title: GET /api/issues returns 380 KB with no pagination, 72% of which is a content field the list UI never reads
findings.location: api/src/routes/issues.ts:126 (SELECT d.content), :99 (content: row.content), :215-224 (ORDER BY with no LIMIT/OFFSET)
findings.evidence: Measured payload 379,907 bytes for 254 issues. Slowest endpoint measured at every concurrency level: P95 38.8 ms at c=10, 94.5 ms at c=25 (headline), 182.0 ms at c=50; P99 208.4 ms at c=50. Throughput saturates at 299 req/s versus 891-900 req/s for the small-payload endpoints, i.e. it is ~3x more expensive per request. `grep -n "LIMIT\|OFFSET" api/src/routes/issues.ts` returns no matches. Postgres measurement: the content column is 138 kB of the 191 kB of live issue text (72.3%). The issues list UI never dereferences it — grep for `.content` across web/src/components/IssuesList.tsx and web/src/pages/Issues.tsx returns only unrelated prop names and comments, no data use.
findings.hypothesis: Response-serialization bound, not query bound: the handler batches its associations correctly (getBelongsToAssociationsBatch, api/src/utils/document-crud.ts:148-180, one ANY($1) query — no N+1), and the row count is only 254, so the ~300 req/s ceiling and the near-perfectly linear latency-vs-concurrency curve point at JSON.stringify plus socket writes of 381 KB per response on a single Node process (no clustering in api/src/index.ts).
findings.estimatedImpact: Dropping content from the list projection shrinks the payload ~2.6x and should cut P95 at c=25 from 94.5 ms to roughly 35-40 ms (~55-60%), clearing the >=20% improvement target on this endpoint alone. Adding LIMIT/OFFSET additionally caps growth, which is currently linear: at 10x seed volume this response is ~3.8 MB.

findings.title: No response compression anywhere in the API; the largest payload ships 15.4x larger than it needs to
findings.location: api/src/app.ts (no compression middleware registered); api/package.json (compression is not a dependency)
findings.evidence: Measured: curl with `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` against /api/issues returns `Content-Length: 379907` and no `Content-Encoding` response header, i.e. the body is sent uncompressed even when the client advertises support. gzip -9 of the identical body is 24,627 bytes (15.4x). Same measurement for the other key endpoints: /api/documents 293,891 -> 27,749 (10.5x), /api/documents?type=wiki 37,868 -> 4,559 (8.3x), /api/team/assignments 22,655 -> 1,750 (12.9x), /api/weeks 4,351 -> 918 (4.7x).
findings.hypothesis: compression middleware was never added. The gap is invisible in local development and in this benchmark because loopback transfer is effectively free, so it never shows up in a localhost latency number — it only costs real users on a WAN link.
findings.estimatedImpact: On a 10 Mbps agency link the /api/issues body alone is ~304 ms of transfer; gzip reduces that to ~20 ms. IMPORTANT for compare mode: enabling gzip will NOT reduce P95 measured over loopback and may raise it slightly (compression CPU is added while transfer time stays ~0). This fix must be validated over a bandwidth-shaped link or by payload size, not by re-running this localhost benchmark. Also verify whether CloudFront edge compression already masks part of this in the deployed stack.

findings.title: Command palette (cmd+K) re-downloads the entire 294 KB document corpus on every open, bypassing the react-query cache
findings.evidence: The useEffect is keyed on [open] and calls plain apiGet('/api/documents') into local useState, bypassing the queryClient (staleTime 5 min, gcTime 24 h) entirely, so every palette open is a cold fetch. Measured payload 293,891 bytes for all 500 documents; browser trace confirms exactly one GET /api/documents of 293,891 bytes fired on opening the palette. Endpoint P95 34.0 ms at c=10, 75.7 ms at c=25, 146.5 ms at c=50; throughput ceiling 299 req/s. GET /api/documents has no LIMIT/OFFSET (api/src/routes/documents.ts:94-154).
findings.hypothesis: Search is implemented as client-side filtering over the full corpus (groupedDocuments useMemo at :169) rather than a server-side query. A /api/search router exists but its only frontend consumer is /api/search/mentions for editor @-autocomplete (web/src/components/editor/MentionExtension.ts:23), so no server-side document search is reachable from the UI.
findings.estimatedImpact: Cost grows linearly with workspace size — at 10x seed volume each cmd+K press transfers ~2.9 MB. Routing the palette through the existing search router plus react-query caching removes a 294 KB fetch from an interactive keystroke path and returns 1 of the 100 req/min production budget per open.

findings.title: Dashboard issues one request per active week for standups (client-side N+1)
findings.evidence: Promise.all over activeWeeks issuing GET /api/weeks/${sprint.id}/standups per week. Browser trace of the dashboard flow: 12 API requests total, of which 5 are this fan-out, each returning exactly 2 bytes ("[]") — 10 bytes of payload spread over 5 round trips. The parent GET /api/weeks is itself cheap (4,351 bytes, P95 14.2 ms at c=25). Request count grows with the number of active weeks, not with a constant.
findings.hypothesis: No batch endpoint exists for standups-by-week, so the client loops. Each week also re-enters authMiddleware, paying the full per-request auth cost (see API-6) for a 2-byte result.
findings.estimatedImpact: A single GET /api/weeks/standups?week_ids=... collapses 5 round trips into 1, cutting the dashboard from 12 to 8 requests (-33%) and reclaiming budget against API-1. Cross-reference: the server-side query-count counterpart belongs to db-query-audit (DB).

findings.title: Every authenticated request — including every GET — performs a session UPDATE, making all reads writers
findings.location: api/src/middleware/auth.ts:203-206 (UPDATE sessions SET last_activity), :126-133 (session SELECT); api/src/middleware/visibility.ts:6-24 (per-handler isWorkspaceAdmin)
findings.evidence: Read of the middleware: every authenticated request runs SELECT session JOIN users, then unconditionally UPDATE sessions SET last_activity = $1 WHERE id = $2, and each handler then runs its own isWorkspaceAdmin/getVisibilityContext SELECT — at least 3 queries before any endpoint-specific work. Measured floor: GET /api/documents/:id returns only 2,195 bytes from one indexed primary-key lookup yet still costs P50 2.6 ms / P95 4.8 ms at c=10 and P50 14.3 ms / P95 46.2 ms at c=50. Latency scales linearly with concurrency on all six endpoints (c=10 -> c=50 P50 ratios 4.8x-5.5x for a 5x concurrency increase), so this is saturation, not lock convoy — the shared-row write is not yet the binding constraint at this volume.
findings.hypothesis: Sliding-session bookkeeping is done inline and unthrottled, even though the cookie refresh right below it (auth.ts:209-212) is already throttled to 60 s. The pg pool is capped at max: 10 in dev / 20 in production (api/src/db/client.ts:20), so at concurrency 50 requests queue for connections while each holds one to perform a write that changes nothing meaningful 99% of the time.
findings.estimatedImpact: Throttling the last_activity write to the same ~60 s threshold already used for the cookie removes one write per request, roughly a third of the query count on cheap endpoints, and stops every GET from generating WAL. It is also a prerequisite for ever serving reads from a replica. Cross-reference: per-flow query counts belong to db-query-audit (DB).
